utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Joanna Korner and Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances, Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: David Cunningham with John Ackerman and Aleksandar Vujic. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Just a very brief one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In light of the fact that we're moving through our case and in light of the fact that the Defence would like to get an idea of how much time we're going to have to do our final brief, we would like to suggest to the Court to perhaps have a scheduling conference so we can get an idea of -- of what the Chambers' intentions are with respect to the intervals between the close of evidence and the submission of briefs and then arguments. That will help us plan our Christmas holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we had discussed that some time back. I'm not quite sure that I have the document here with me. I have, but it's not completely updated. But I have got some notes on it. This is the last one. Combined with it, and I'm saying this to give you some advance -- not warning, but some advance notice, it's still our intention to try and have -- to visit the area, an on-site. And I have discussed it already with the Registrar, and I have an indication that it should be possible. What I would like from your part in order to start planning and also to submit the requests in writing as I suggested it should be done -- I mean, the intention was to submit it in writing today. But I haven't had time to discuss with my two colleagues, and also I would like to have feedback from both of you. If there are sites that you are particularly -- you as Prosecution, you as Defence, that you are particularly -- not just interested, but that you consider them to be a must that should be seen, so that we will take that in all due consideration. If you can come back -- yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in some measures -- I mean, I'm going to support what Mr. Cunningham said. I think it is quite useful before we break for Christmas to have a look at the overall schedule. With regards to a site visit, Your Honour, that may need discussion, (a), between the Defence and ourselves; and (b), I'm not at the moment quite clear whether -- is it Your Honours' intention to go off your own, as it were, or is it meant to be, as Your Honour will be familiar with, a jury visit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly that's what I had in mind, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which case counsel for both sides would be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it doesn't go down well with either of you, please let us know. But that's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that seems eminently right to me and then we can discuss the procedures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- that could be followed at a later stage. I would certainly encourage Your Honours as I have all along --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and I have discussed it with the Registrar, and it should be -- obviously we have to discuss logistics and other matters, as you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I would like to have a feedback from both of you as to particular places that you consider useful that this Tribunal -- this Trial Chamber should visit. Then obviously we will use our own judgement to decide where to go. But we will do it the way I am used to do it in a trial, so there would be everyone present, accused is to be excluded obviously for obviously reasons in this particular case. But we'll have it with both sides, both sides being present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it would be helpful, then, if we were to, perhaps -- Your Honours have to put in a request with the places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We discussed it with the Registrar, and the best way to go about it is to submit it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because obviously it has to be processed. Other requests have to be made by the Registrar to other departments in the Tribunal, and the money should be there. So it's not a problem of finding --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judging by our experience, Your Honour, the Republika Srpska liaison officer requires six weeks' notice of anything. But Your Honour, would it help if perhaps Mr. Ackerman and I were to meet after the sitting and discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I am mentioning this. Because, obviously it will -- it's not my intention, and this we have discussed, Judge Janu and Judge Taya already, it's not my intention to have this before the end of your case obviously. And anyway, it should not be held in a way which would obstruct, or which would -- you know, I mean, defeat the whole plan that we have to economise on time as much as we could. So what I would like you to do is to have a short discussion amongst yourselves first, and then keep in mind the following: That I'm assuming that the -- at the worst scenario is that the Defence will finish its case on the 13th of February. That's what I'm assuming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's probably fairly close, Your Honour. We've worked on the witness list since we were last here. We've cut it down some more even. I think that's probably realistic number at this point. Even if we were to -- the only reason -- let me say this: The expert, Professor Shoup, because of his late entrance on to the scene would not have his report ready and be prepared to testify before the 9th, I think, of February is when we've scheduled him. Even if we finish other evidence prior to that time, we are going to have to wait for Professor Shoup. But I don't see that being more than three or four days probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then the idea was to have one week after the close of the Defence case, an entire week, for both of you to prepare yourselves for the rebuttal and the rejoinder. Then it had been planned that one week would be taken by the Prosecution for presenting their rebuttal, and one week by the Defence for your rejoinder, Mr. Ackerman. And then the idea was to have four weeks for the preparation of the closing statements with the Prosecution brief due 30th March and Defence brief due April 1st. This may not be... No, no, no, it is correct, yeah. And then the closing arguments we had dedicated or we had planned to dedicate an entire week for closing arguments, Prosecution and Defence together in one week, 5th to 9th April. So keeping that in mind, keeping that in mind, we need to try and fit in an on-site visit. So...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment, I mean obviously things can change over the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's taken for granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I doubt very much that we'll require a week for rebuttal evidence, if at all. It may be just be documents. Equally, I'd very much doubt, given we're putting in written closing briefs that the final address would probably, although I'm always wrong in this, take just over one day. Possibly going into a second, but that's it. Your Honour, can I just ask, though: Again I think Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Cunningham told us last week that we would have the new list, the full list now of witnesses by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we got it. And the summaries we would like as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were supposed to be working on this Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was my understanding. My discussion with Ms. Korner was that I would have the list completed before we go on break, and that's still my intention. We're not finished with it yet. We're working on it. And we've got some communication going on with Banja Luka and we're not yet to give a final list, but we're close. And we'll certainly have it before the break starts. In fact, hopefully if we can have some kind of Status Conference later on this week, we will have it prepared by that time. Maybe Wednesday or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Wednesday we are sitting in the afternoon. So we could have a Status Conference in the morning if it's -- late in the morning, if that's fine with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on that note, and this is purely personal, it's medical. I have a great deal of difficulty arranging an appointment. It's at lunchtime on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That shouldn't be a problem, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that it may be that this witness will not take the full three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I read his statement, the statement that he gave to you. I don't see why we should be here three days, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we could, perhaps, if we finish early afternoon on Wednesday, then have a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's agree first that there will be a Status Conference between now and end of business on Wednesday, or even it could also be Thursday, for all that matters. We are available, the three of us. We don't have any other commitments, except this case this week. So let's play it by the ear and as soon as there is time available for the -- to hold a Status Conference, we'll hold a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, can I confirm, we're sitting tomorrow afternoon as well, it's tomorrow and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, tomorrow and Wednesday afternoon. If -- unless we can shift it to the morning but I think it's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand there are cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's very difficult because I tried, Madam Chuqing tried, and even someone else tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thursday and Friday we are likely to be the only trial sitting there, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just Your Honour, something I would ask Your Honours to consider. You mentioned the Prosecution brief would be due 30 March and the Defence brief 1 April, that gives like us one day to read their brief and reply to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The plan we had before was two days, but we are flexible on that, Mr. Ackerman. It's not going to make a difference to us, I suppose, if we shift it from the 1st to the 2nd or to the 3rd. So don't -- let's leave that to the Status Conference that we will hold, but don't let it ruin your sleep or your digestion, Mr. Ackerman, because we will find a solution for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you learned that from me. I kept telling you "Don't worry about it, Judge." Now you're telling me not to worry. Don't worry, be happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can we bring in the witness. Yes, let's go into private session for a while, just for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no protective measures here, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is this your witness, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Sajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence in the -- in this ongoing trial against Radoslav Brdjanin. You have been summoned here as a Defence witness, and our Rules require that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. This is basically equivalent to an oath that you would take in your own jurisdiction. The text of the solemn declaration is going to be handed to you now by Madam Usher. Could you please stand up, read that text, that solemn declaration aloud, and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal that you will testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sajic. You're going to be examined first through a series of questions by Mr. Cunningham, who is appearing for Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Cunningham will then be followed by Mr. Nicholls, by Mr. Nicholls, for the Prosecution. My suggestion to you is that you try to be as concise as possible in your answers, and to the point. You have a duty to answer truthfully and fully, but also to the point. So don't try to volunteer information that is not being asked from you. Otherwise, you'll be here the entire week. Did I make myself understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just before we start, could we again move the ELMO just a little bit because I can't see the witness well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And it doesn't look like the right-hand microphone is on, at least from my angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Cunningham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Milorad Sajic. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday when we met in your hotel room, I left you with a binder full of exhibits that we will use today. Did you bring that exhibit book, that binder, with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead and get it out and have it at the ready in case you need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but this is the second time Mr. Cunningham has said this. Can I just make a point out of absolute caution: If witnesses are being given binders of documents to take with them wherever they're staying, are we sure that they're not taking with them confidential, under seal documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The documents that are in there are the exhibits that are being proposed to be used today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. My concern is taking them to a hotel, possibly leaving them somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All of the exhibits today are public documents, and I have been cautioned with respect to -- and can we go into private session for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher, could you bring the witness in, please. Mr. Sajic, my apologies to you. It was not our intention to bring you here and let you stay in a room waiting for us to discuss certain matters, certain issues that we had to deal with before we could proceed with your testimony. It would have been easier for me if these problems involved you, but they do not really involve you, so you don't have to worry about it. Let's proceed now, but I wanted you to know how sorry I am that you had to stay in there waiting for almost two hours now, almost two hours. But we couldn't avoid this. So I'm sorry. Mr. Cunningham is going to question you on the events that took place in Banja Luka in 1992 and other events. And he will then be followed by Ms. Korner, as I explained to you earlier. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, we got so far as confirming what your name was. Let me ask you, what municipality were you born in?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Srbac Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which municipality do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend secondary school at? Which municipality or municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Part in Banja Luka and part in Srbac. That's where I completed my secondary education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing your secondary education, did you go to university?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend university at?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: School for economics in Banja Luka, and political sciences in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have more than -- do you have a university diploma, a university degree?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a BA in economy, and my other occupation is a teacher of national defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say a teacher of national defence, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: This is a special department at the political sciences faculty, defence and protection. Once you finish that school, you obtain a diploma to certify that you are a professor of defence and protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of any political parties?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Until 1990, I had been a member of the League of Communists. I was never a member of any other party later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you do compulsory military service as a younger man?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you complete your military service?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: 1968 and 1969. It lasts for a year. It was half/half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completion of your compulsory military service in 1969, did you remain in the military or did you enter civilian life?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I was back in civilian life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us very briefly your employment, what sort of jobs you've worked at, say, from leaving the service in 1969 up until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I worked in Laktasi for the Territorial Defence staff until 1979, or 1978, after which I worked in Banja Luka for a year or so with the district staff and then later with the municipal Territorial Defence staff, from 1981. In Banja Luka, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work continuously for the TO in either one municipality or another from 1969 or 1970 up until 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in 1992, were you commander of the Banja Luka TO, the municipality TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also the secretary to the regional secretariat for national defence during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, for several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you also a member of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in 1992, were you -- did you become an officer in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave military service?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In 1996, after I had been demobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your demobilisation in 1996, did you start working in the civilian sector again?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's your current position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: At the Palace Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your position at the Palace Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I'm the manager of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going -- you told us you were the commander of the Banja Luka Territorial Defence. Tell us again when you came to Banja Luka to start working with the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I joined the municipal staff in 1981, and the district staff prior to that, in 1979.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the 1980s, were you promoted, rise up the chain, if you will, in the Banja Luka TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of promotions did you receive in the 1980s while working at the Banja Luka TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I was the chief of the operations organ, the assistant for logistics, and after that the commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you appointed to be the commander of the Banja Luka TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I was appointed in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it that you were appointed? What was the procedure that led to your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: At the time, the rules said that the municipal assembly should appoint the TO commanders pursuant to proposals by the president of the assembly, and an opinion of the commander of the republican staff of the Territorial Defence would be needed to make the appointment. I was proposed by the president of the assembly and nominated and appointed by the assembly itself at one of its sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your appointment approved by the republican staff of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your appointment follow the procedure that was set forth in the law of Yugoslavia existing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk about the responsibilities that -- of the TO. Under the -- according to the law of national defence in the former Yugoslavia, was the republican -- let me rephrase the question. According to the law of national defence in the former Yugoslavia, were the republican authorities responsible for providing certain things, items, to the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The law on the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, there were two components to that. One was the JNA as the unified armed force of the entire state of Yugoslavia, and the other component was the TO. That was organised across the republics and even provinces, I believe. The republics had the duty to help with organising training, preparing and assisting their own republican TO within the framework of the duties they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the municipalities responsible for anything with respect to the TO; that is, did they have duties and obligations with respect to the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The municipalities were a bit like the republics, but at a lower level. They had the duty to organise, to recruit, to train, to finance as far as their municipality was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were the commander of the TO simply for the Municipality of Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a Banja Luka region of the TO? I guess I should say, was there in 1991 when you assumed the position a region that you were part of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before and after, there were regional staffs, or rather district staffs of the TO for certain areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You had the Banja Luka staff for the Banja Luka area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who was the commander for the region when you assumed your position in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: It was Colonel Milan Krneta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ultimately replaced in -- sometime in 1991 or in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in the summer of 1991 that he retired and was replaced by Lieutenant Colonel Petar Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- these two individuals your immediate supervisors?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would be over the regional commander? Who would be the next up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: There was the republican staff of the Territorial Defence. These were practically sections or branch offices, subordinate offices, of the republican staff which was in charge of the entire republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, the commander was General Drago Vukosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And going again up the chain of command after this last general you cited, who would be next in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: For the use of units in combat, it would have been the general staff of the armed forces. I think the man in charge would have been General Kadijevic at the time, for the use of those units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And above him would have been who?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The presidency, the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were appointed with the municipal assembly -- appointed by the municipal assembly. Did you know Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By virtue of your position as commander of the TO in the municipality, did you have a professional working relationship with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: My people and myself, the people that answered to me, were employed and financed by the Municipality of Banja Luka, as was the case with all other municipal organs. So this work relationship went towards the president of the assembly and the president of the executive board. Some organs answered directly to the president of the assembly, and some to the presidents of the executive board. And Mr. Radic was the president of the assembly at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you answer to Mr. Radic or the president of the executive council on issues?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: As a rule, to President Radic because he was also the president of the defence council at the municipal level. As far as the finances were concerned, the whole thing went through the executive council. These functions intertwined slightly, but that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "these functions intertwined," which functions are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the financing of all the different bodies, the executive council of the municipality was in charge, and they made budget proposals for the municipality. All the requests for equipment, for salaries, for any materiel equipment, this all went through the executive council, and the executive council would have been in charge of that. As for preparation, training, mobilisation, different courses, training courses and seminars, as well as the equipment, this would always be discussed at the Defence council and the president of this counsel, rather, the chairman, was the president of the municipality. This was a peculiar situation because everybody answered to -- all the different bodies answered to the president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You bring up a good point. You said you answered to the president of the executive council. Did the president of the executive council have the competence to issue a binding order to you, commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In addition to trying to keep me within the budget, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was the link between you and the municipality financial, or was it more than that? And just so you understand what I'm saying, by "financial," I mean the fact that they paid and your staff salary and pensions and insurance and things like that, did it go beyond that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the president of the executive council not having the competence to issue an order to you. What about the president of the municipality? Did he have the competence to issue an order to you in 1991, 1992 that you would be obligated to follow?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you as commander of the TO obliged to follow the conclusions and decisions of municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: These almost never applied to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: They didn't apply to the use of units which was the most important thing. If you had to save money, then everyone had to save money, financially speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned it earlier in your testimony that you were -- you mentioned the notion, the topic of municipal defence councils. What is a municipal defence council?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The National Defence Council for the municipality was an advisory body, an advisory body, reviewing issues related to organisation and preparation as well as the achievements in the area of the Territorial Defence, the National Defence, the secretariat for National Territorial Defence, civilian protection, police, and the like. But only as an advisory body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this according to the law of the former Yugoslavia? Did the law of the former Yugoslavia provide for this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The law of the former Yugoslavia and of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina did provide for this. This council would be appointed by the municipality, and the law provided for the various positions that would be part of the council, positions that the council was made up of. Those were not deputies, the people appointed. These positions were legally prescribed, and then some of -- some more appointments would additionally be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by virtue of your appointment to commander of the TO in Banja Luka in 1991, did you also become a member of this National Defence Council for the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the TO under the law would have been a member. The president of the assembly would have the president. And the secretary of the secretariat for National Defence would have the secretary to this council. And there are a number of other positions, but in answer to your question, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serving on this National Defence Council in Banja Luka with you, were there any members of the active military?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: As far as the composition of the council was concerned, the law provided for a representative of the JNA, which meant one of the commands of the JNA. Not all the municipalities had a JNA presence, so usually those would be representatives from the highest command. And this was the case in Banja Luka also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who from the army or from the highest command was on the National Defence Council with you in Banja Luka in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In 1991, Uzelac, while he was the corps commander; and in 1992, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of General Talic, in 19 -- at the time he was the corps commander, did he attend these National Defence Council meetings in person, or did he send a representative? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: As a rule, both commanders attended meetings whenever they could. Sometimes, though, they would send their representatives or an authorised officer, so there were times when he was not personally in attendance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, 1992, how often were these advisory board, National Defence Councils meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Not too often really. Not very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I appreciate the answer, but that doesn't really tell us much. Did they meet once a month, once a year, once a decade? Give us an idea, please, how often the meetings were.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Whenever the need arose, but I reckon it would have been two or three times a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And who determined when the need arose? Who made the decision to call a meeting of these National Defence Councils?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The secretary for National Defence, the secretary of the secretariat for National Defence, who was also the secretary of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Council for National Defence. He would prepare the material for the sessions, and when there were issues to be reviewed, for example, reports on recruitment, reports on mobilisation, reports on civilian protection, he would make proposals to the president of the council, the president of the municipality, to convene a session. The necessary materials would then be forwarded, and that's how it was done. They raised issues that the council then reviewed, according to a regular procedure. Throughout the year, two or three times, the law did provide for this, and that's how it was done. Reports on the work of the secretariat and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I forgot to ask this question of you earlier, and I'm sorry for that. You told us that there were members of the army on the council. Was -- were people from the security structures, from the police, also on the council?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Civilian police?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the civilian police's presence on the National Defence Council by virtue of the law -- by virtue of the law which designated who would serve on the National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at these meetings that you attended, were you - and I'm speaking of you as the commander of the TO - were you ever ordered by the municipal authorities to undertake or do a specific act?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: You mean the council, the council provided guidelines and instructions as concerned the Territorial Defence, and these instructions and guidelines would then be considered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I guess what I'm getting at is at any of these meetings, these National Defence Council meetings that you attended, did any municipal authority order you, direct you, command you to undertake a specific act? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the municipal authorities have the competence to enter such an order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, with respect to the -- what I'll call the active-duty military and the police, did the municipal authorities ever, during these meetings, ever issue a direct order to those entities requiring them to undertake a certain or specific act?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: There could have been guidelines, but the municipal authorities did not have the power to issue any orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were commander of the municipality TO, did it undergo some very serious restructuring and reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In 1992, there was the restructuring of TO units in the infantry brigade. Up to then, up to 1992, everything had been the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to stop here for two or three minutes. I need to leave the courtroom. And I will be back in two or three minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that everything remained the same until 1992. Did something happen in the spring of 1992 that prompted this reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In the spring, the Army of Republika Srpska was set up, and the TO became part of it. That was what the restructuring of the TO was about, towards the establishment of that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date that the VRS was formally established?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I believe on the 12th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as commander of the TO involved in this reorganisation, did the efforts at reorganisation begin before or after 12 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the changes that were undertaken with respect to the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: TO, as it was, became four light infantry brigades that were then set up and placed under the command of the corps, or rather the brigade development unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to Banja Luka, how many light -- I think you've already answered that. Was this something that was done overnight, or did this take work to form these four light infantry brigades?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Each attempt at reorganisation of the units needs time. This was about making units bigger, transforming them from the platoon squads and companies that they were into brigades, and this required time. This took some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is it that it took time to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: It took time to make these units into bigger units, to set up brigade commands, to make the platoons and squads part of the companies, and then to reorganise, restructure the whole thing and set it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this take place, this reorganisation that you've just described, did that start in earnest on or about the date that the VRS was officially proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Not on the same date. It never quite happens at the same time as anything else. There was an order several days later pursuant to which this started, and I think this was completed by the 15th or 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How much time -- how many hours per day would you think that you spent in handling or helping out on this reorganisation? Between the time it started and June 15th 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not getting a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can the interpreters repeat the interpretation, please, so that we can check whether Mr. Cunningham -- whether this is a fault specific to Mr. Cunningham only?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The usual working hours, was what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm back online, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, interpreters, and thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the normal working hours for you in May and June of 1992 were what, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question because I don't think it made it to you. You said you spent your normal working hours involved in this reorganisation. What were your normal working hours back in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Normal working hours, well, to work eight hours or perhaps ten hours a day, but this implied that the units that were across the territory of the municipality, that these units were to be grouped in larger units. And from the units, that companies should be formed and -- both in terms of organisation, that they should be finalised and form companies that, of course, had to be then various -- the staff had to be found, and this was the procedure of work, not only my procedure of work, but of all the other commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how big a staff did you have to assist you in this reorganisation effort?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, my staff was -- included about 14, 15 people, and as such it was engaged on such duties. It had certain departments which were in charge of such affairs, organisation, the operational unit and other units. And this was all part of the reorganisation process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us you had a staff of 14 to 15 people. What was the ethnicity -- ethnicities of those 14 to 15 people that worked for you in May and April of 19 -- excuse me, in May and June 1992 when this reorganisation was being done?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the composition, ethnic composition, was multinational. Well, it wasn't the same percentage situation as in 1991. There were certain elements wanting to remain and stay there and work there, and other ethnicities other than the Serb also remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But to get back to my question, of the 14 to 15 people that worked for you in May and June 1992, specifically how many of them were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's slightly less than 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were there Croats working among this group of non-Serbs that were working with you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that some remained until the end, and then joined the light brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Muslims? Did you have any Bosniaks working for you during this two-month period in May and June of 1992 while you're doing the reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the place in your testimony. You said: "Certain elements wanted to remain and stay there and work there, and other ethnicities other than the Serbs also remained." Why did certain elements want to leave? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: They had no reason to leave because of the staff or the command. But because of the political situation in Banja Luka, they -- some remained, some left. But not very many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me clear up this one final point. You said: "... some remained, some left. But not very many." Within your staff, how many non-Serbs left during this time period we're talking about in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the names. I can't remember them. But the atmosphere was such that many remained. No one was forcing them. But I can't remember individually the names of these persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've talked about this reorganisation that was done in part to incorporate the TO into the VRS. Did this reorganisation require that you have conversations and/or meetings with the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: For the reorganisation of the TO at that particular point in time, it was, in fact, a short period of time, and it was very fragmented. The TO organised on the basis of local communities, and much time was needed, and there were instructions and orders and discussion revolved around those issues, how this should be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm not faulting you for this, but I don't think you answered the question of conversations with the corps commander. Did that happen? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially when appointing the commanders of the brigade. He was appointed by the commander of the corps, and the TO would propose who. They didn't -- it was necessary to adjust these appointees who would be appointed commander of the brigades. And So this was a topic of discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that this reorganisation was going on, where did you spend the bulk of your time? Was it devoted to reorganisation and everything that went with it, or to something else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, a lot of my time was devoted to that. That was one of my primary tasks, the reorganisation of the total TO. So most of my time was devoted to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened with the four light infantry brigades once they were formed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Four light infantry brigades, well, the reorganisation lasted until June 15th, and then they were formed, these brigades, and became part of the corps, of the 1st Krajina Corps under the command of the -- the commander of the corps appointed the commander of those brigades, a group of officers which -- who commanded the brigade, the four light infantry brigades. So the staff -- the municipal staff ceased to exist, and my function as -- in the Territorial Defence stopped as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us about the date of this reorganisation starting shortly after the official proclamation of the VRS on 12 May 1992. At some time during the first week of May 1992, did you become aware you had been appointed to the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember the date that you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I remember when I was invited and informed of this appointment. I think it was on May 5th, according to the council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did your efforts, the time that you spent to the reorganisation of the municipality TO, did that interfere with your ability to attend meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was pretty leading. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he's already made his point, but in the future I'd rather the -- those be -- when we get into this area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Usually as you know, I do not interfere unless there is an objection. And I think the objection is well founded. I invite Mr. Cunningham to rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the ARK Crisis Staff, were there meetings -- let me back up. Were there meetings called of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect, if any, did your -- did the reorganisation and the time that you were spending with the reorganisation have on your ability to attend ARK Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it limited my possibilities of attending those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll come back -- we'll come to this again in the future. But if you missed a meeting of the ARK Crisis Staff, were you ever individually threatened or sanctioned for failing to attend?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very early in your testimony, you told us that at one time during the spring and summer of 1992, you were the regional -- you were the secretary for the regional secretariat for National Defence. Do you remember when you got that position, what date that was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, end of April I was appointed, and I took over the duty following this cessation of the TO and the reorganisation following June 15th. So I partially had that duty, but not professionally, not -- I wasn't paid for that, and I didn't have my working hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When did you start devoting time, if any, to the duties that went with being the secretary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the secretary of the National Defence, it is actually a related or similar function which existed in times of peace at the level of certain groups in the municipality. And at the time, the republic secretary for National Defence had his own department in -- or unit in individual cities which covered certain -- this was Mostar, Tuzla, Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go ahead and stop you there. Because I think you misunderstood my question. What I asked you was: In light of the fact that you were dealing with the reorganisation of the TO, when did you actually start devoting time, if any, to the duties that went with being the secretary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Following the reorganisation of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this position, the secretary for the -- excuse me. The position that you were appointed to on 27 April 1992, was that a new position under the law?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: It was called secretary, but before that, was the assistant of the Defence for the region of Banja Luka. This unit, it was a branch actually of the Ministry of Defence, had existed in the past, and the deputy at the time for Banja Luka, his name was Cecerevic [phoen], Ranko. So when the council was formed, it appointed me secretary for the National Defence of the region which implied the function that had the same sort of competencies as in the past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the actual position that had the same sort of competence in the past was what? What was the name of that position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Deputy minister for National Defence for the region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: It was a function of the deputy minister for National Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your position, the one that you got appointed to, was it a brand-new position that had just been developed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I explained this clearly. I was appointed to the function of secretary. This name did not exist in the past but were the same as those of deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction when you got appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, sincerely speaking, I wasn't happy about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Because I had -- I was very busy in the sense of Territorial Defence. It was a duplication of functions, and I couldn't cover everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your job responsibilities as -- in this new position that you were appointed to on 27 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: My obligation was to be a link between the Ministry of Defence of the Socialist Republic of B and H, and the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was called the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was a link between the municipal secretariat and the ministry. It was a link, a bypass, transmitting communications, orders, providing assistance to the municipal secretariats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did your job duties include anything involving recruitment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the function itself in the secretariat for National Defence was before the war, during the war, and now more or less the same, which means that it was a job to keep records of the age of young men coming to serve in the army, that means recruitment, recruitment, recruitment of conscripts. Then filling in the ranks with reservists in the JNA units, and later on this was being done in the -- within the VRS. Then filling in and actually finding all that was required in terms of vehicles and so forth. Briefly, this was the kind of job responsibility, and this was being done from the level of the ministries down to the level of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your job have a civil defence or civil protection aspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just to check -- there's something -- I want to see if this is a translation error. It's about page 52 -- I've lost it. 52/1, the witness has described the municipal secretariat, and being municipal secretariat and a link to the municipal secretariat. And earlier the testimony -- and I believe it's -- he used the term regional secretariat. So I don't know if we're talking about the region or municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll put it to the witness myself. To the question of what were your job responsibilities, and this imposition on 27th April, you said: "My obligation was to be a link between the Ministry of Defence of the Socialist Republic of B and H, and the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was called the Serb Republic. It was a link between the municipal secretariat and the ministry." Is that correct? Or was it a link between the regional secretariat and the ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. My function was to be a link between the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska and the municipal secretariat. So the Defence Ministry and the municipal secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have to stop here so that we can change the tapes. I suggest a break of about 5 minutes. And then we will stop for 30 minutes or 25 minutes at half past 12.00. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.53 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you want to wait for Ms. Korner or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can start, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a couple of moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before our break, Mr. Sajic, I asked you whether your job as secretary for the secretariat for National Defence had a civil defence or civil protection component, and you didn't get a chance to answer that. So could you do that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that civil defence, civil protection component of your job?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Civil protection means that there are units of civilian protection that can be used to take care of the population under a wide range of different circumstances. You have first aid units there; you have vet units; you have sanitation units; you have fire fighting units, all sorts of civil units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- as the secretary for the regional secretariat for National Defence, did you play any role in mobilisation, or did your office play any role in mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: This was one of its major roles of the secretariat, mobilisation, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, how did that work with respect to the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Mobilisation of units before and now was done through the Defence secretariat. Now those are sections or branches offices, but back then they used to be secretariats. Commands submit requests for certain units to be mobilised, and then the secretariats, by couriers, forward the call-ups to people's home addresses whenever persons are being mobilised if. Need is to mobilise vehicles or cattle or other materiel resources that the unit is entitled to, no matter whether those are privately owned or owned by a company, if assigned to those units, these requests are also carried out. This roughly speaking is the way it's done. A call-up is sent. People are told where to report to, according to their assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that commands submit requests for certain units to be mobilised. To whom would the command submit these requests? Would they come to you or another secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The requests would go -- well, depending on the level of the units being mobilised. If it was general mobilisation, this would have been ordered by the Defence Ministry. If individual units are being mobilised, where individual units are being mobilised, one is and one isn't, so to say, then the requests are mostly sent down to the secretariats where the recruitment is being done because all the files were and still are with the municipalities as to recruitment. As for mobilisation, general mobilisation, this is always ordered by the ministry and submitted via what today we call branch offices or sections, recruitment offices. At that time, it was the secretariat for the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That's as far as mobilisation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the requests are mostly sent down to secretariats where the recruitment is being done because all the files were and still are with the municipalities. I take it that means that you would -- these would go to the national secretariat on the municipal level. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In your capacity as the secretary, were you obligated, were you required, to carry out the orders of the Minister for Defence for the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you answer to when you were wearing the hat as secretariat for the National Defence for the ARK? Who was your immediate supervisor? Who did you answer to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: In terms of defence, in terms of how the jobs were carried out, it would have been the republican Defence minister. Within the organisation itself, the president of the ARK council, the executive council of Krajina. But as far as mobilisation was concerned and those requests to be carried out, it had to do with the Defence Ministry. This was for a brief period of time only. We couldn't even -- I'm talking about two months, a mere two months. And later on, sections or departments were set up where you knew for sure who answered to whom and for what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these two months that you worked in this capacity, did anyone on the municipal -- excuse me, on the regional level have the authority -- let me back up. In the two months that you worked in this capacity, did any civilian person on the regional level have the authority to order a mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did anyone on the regional or municipal level have the authority or competence to order you to undertake any act while you were wearing this hat? And I'm talking about the regional or municipal civilian level.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'd like for you to do is I'd like for you to open up the exhibit book that I have for you, and I'd like you to go to the tab -- it should be the very first tab in there marked Exhibit P153. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a decision dated 16 April 1992, and who is it signed by on the second page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the person who signed it? Tell us who it is.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The Minister of National Defence, Bogdan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of hierarchy or chain of command, who is he in relation to your position at the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: My superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive this decision dated 16 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And upon receipt of this decision, what did you do with it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the decision, I issued an order on mobilisation in ARK Krajina territory. I forwarded this to the municipal secretariats for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you go now to document -- the next document which I think is 167. That should be the next one there. Do you recognise this document that's in front of you, P167?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the decision that you talked about regarding general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the source of this document, P167? Was it the Ministry of Defence or the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we were to compare this exhibit, this document dated 4 May 1992, with the previous one, P153 dated 16 April 1992, it appears to me that there's also something in there about disarmament. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just say for the record this 4th May document is also P1182 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1128"], which is an updated version, corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Exhibit P153 dealt only with mobilisation. Disarmament has been added on to this. Could you tell us how and why this discussion -- an explanation with regard to disarmament of paramilitary formations is added to your order. How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The intention behind this decision was to assume some of the obligations to disarm units, paramilitary units, and those who were in possession of unlawful weapons. We're talking about the month of May, and some of the units were already on front or in Croatia. Those had by and large returned by this time. Secondly, this had been going on for several months, and in major towns such as Banja Luka, even in smaller towns, people had begun to emerge who in a manner of speaking belonged to no one, not the JNA, not the Territorial Defence. Paramilitaries. Very often those were deserters, and some were even prone to crime. There was a need to have a decision on this to disarm all such units, to call on them to hand over their weapons so that the situation throughout the territory could be placed under control. That was the meaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I ask my next question, I'd like to ask with the Court's person for Mr. Nicholls to repeat that exhibit number because it came out 1128 in the transcript and I think you said 1182.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. 1182 is the corrected version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you both. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back and break down your answer you were talking about. When you talk about these individuals who were in possession of unlawful weapons during May and before, what ethnicity are you concerned with?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's -- well, in fact, we're talking about a number of different nationalities. It wasn't about one ethnic group only, the Serb ethnic group. Back in May, there were people from all the different ethnic groups still in town. No one had left by that time. I'll try to put this briefly. The connection between criminals on the one hand or those who did not observe the law, there was no particular discrimination there. There were Croats, Serbs, Muslims on that side, all of them. And the same goes for deserters. In the JNA, from 1991, there had been many recruitments from non-Serbs, from non-Serb groups. For example, there were units where you had up to 30 per cent of persons from other ethnic groups, even those deserters who had left their units, kept their weapons, and kept their uniforms, and used these on a number of occasions to steal anything. There was a lot of confusion being created in town, but everyone, all the different ethnic groups were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was this decision, specifically paragraph number 6 in Exhibit 167, the document that's attributed to you as secretary of the regional secretariat, was this decision intended to disarm only the non-Serb population or was it intended for everyone in illegal possession?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: All the paramilitary units, all the paramilitary formations. Even formations belonging to private entrepreneurs. All of those were meant to be disarmed because some people had begun to profiteer, and some people had begun to set up their own private units as some form of security. All units that were not regular military units were meant to be disarmed. When I say "regular units," at the time I mean the JNA on the one hand and the TO on the other. Everyone else was susceptible to disarmament, no exception made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you issued this decision, was there a problem with Serbian paramilitaries in the area of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: There was a problem. There were paramilitary units, which means that they were not under control. The problem you have immediately is how to uphold public law and order in town. People were walking about carrying weapons, and some of those people had left their units, deserted, and joined paramilitary units layer on. Therefore, their very presence was a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And were you living in Banja Luka in 1992, in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen this problem that you've described, with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: With my own eyes, through my people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would actually -- would the secretariat for National Defence, would that be the entity responsible for disarmament?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: No. No. The police would have been responsible for disarmament. The tasks were issued at the level of the civilian and military police. The military police would have been charged with bringing in any person wearing a uniform, no matter how the specific person had come by the uniform. No matter if it was a regular soldier or a soldier who just totally of his own accord put on a uniform and walked around touting a weapon. This would have been the military police, and the civilian police would have been in charge of doing the same with civilian persons. These were duties which were clearly articulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've talked about these paramilitaries in possession of illegal weapons. Do you have any idea where these weapons came from, how they got these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: To put it mildly, Your Honours, the weapons were very easy to get, especially if we look at the Banja Luka area because units from the area had already been in Croatia and then returned to the Banja Luka general area. Those units were carrying weapons. For a while, they were handing over these weapons, but there were a lot of deserters who deserted with their weapons. Secondly, a lot of weapons had arrived in the Krajina region from the Serb refugees from the Pakrac Valley in Croatia who brought weapons with them on their way back when they came to Krajina. And they even handed these weapons over. These weapons were there for the people to be had. It was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to the date of your order, specifically 1990 and 1991, were weapons distributed by the three parties in the Banja Luka Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which three parties you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- I'm talking about the HDZ, the SDS, and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I have no information who, how much, when. But all the three parties were giving weapons to people. This was generally known. The HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, Your Honours, we're at a good breaking point if that's fine for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to have a break now. We'll have a 25-minute break, and we will resume after that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to go to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I wanted to address the Chamber without the witness being here to make sure that I'm following on your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't realise your client wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think this needs to be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session, and Madam Usher has gone to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were talking about arms and the arming of individuals in the Banja Luka area. When the TO is mobilised, are the people who respond to mobilisation, are they given weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence is mobilised along the lines of the JNA. People are called. They come, and they are issued with arms. And it remains within the unit, as well as other means, resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the TO exist in local communes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: The TO of the Municipality of Banja Luka, as well as other municipalities in B and H exist in local communes and in enterprises. So in local communes and in enterprises, these are units, companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1991 and 1992, were there Croat communes and Muslim communes on the territory of Banja Luka Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, when mobilisation was called, would weapons have been distributed in these Croat and Muslim communes in accordance with the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- can you give the Court an example of a municipality, a non-Serb -- excuse me, a non-Serb commune that was equipped with weapons during mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC
utterances.text: I can speak of the Banja Luka Municipality. There is the example. It's a part near Vrbanja and Veljak. And Vrbanja also received arms. Simic, the village of Simic is also a case in point, purely Croat. It had a unit, and this unit was issued with arms. The Simic local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
